entries.title: The Return of Child Labor
entries.summary: For years I have been haunted by a grainy video I saw in 2023, when I was interviewing poultry processing workers in Green Forest, Arkansas. entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
This story was produced in partnership with the Economic Hardship Reporting Project and supported with a residency from The Bellagio Center.

For years I have been haunted by a grainy video I saw in 2023, when I was interviewing poultry processing workers in Green Forest, Arkansas. In those months I spoke often with the organizer Magaly Licolli, who directs Venceremos, a grassroots organization dedicated to protecting the rights of poultry workers. One day we were sitting in her office in Springdale a few miles from the headquarters of Tyson Foods, the largest meat processing company in the US and, after the Brazilian firm JBS, the second largest in the world. After the subject turned to child labor, she pulled out her phone and showed me footage that another laborer had recorded of two migrant children, fourteen and fifteen years old, working as chicken catchers in a cavernous rural poultry house. The video was dark, but it was clear that they were using their bare hands to grab each chicken by the feet and hurl it into a nearby crate. Their bodies showed up only in outline, like ghostly shadows.

Earlier that year, Licolli told me, six chicken catchers—four adults and two children—had come to Venceremos’s office to seek help. The two minors were asleep when they arrived, she said, “because they hadn’t slept for so many hours.” The catchers explained that the contractor who hired them had denied them a week’s wages because—although they had worked fourteen-to-fifteen-hour days under physically extreme, sometimes dangerous conditions—they hadn’t managed to finish crating 56,000 chickens. According to the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), the catching and cooping of poultry for transport or market is strictly prohibited for minors under the age of sixteen.

After some asking around, Licolli found the name of the contractor, called him, and told him he had to pay the chicken catchers. “Otherwise, I would have involved the Department of Labor,” she told me. The contractor agreed. Licolli drove to Decatur, some thirty miles from Springdale, to pick up the money, and “that’s how that was resolved.”

In the years that followed, I thought back to those teenagers often. Who was the contractor they worked for? How many other minors did that employer hire? How many other children were working dangerous fifteen-hour shifts? In its brevity and ambiguity, their story seemed to show the predicament of so many children laboring in the poultry processing industry and other dangerous jobs across the US. Working in informal arrangements, they have come to rely on advocates like Licolli to push for their rights, sometimes through similarly informal channels. Many of the children she met in Arkansas, she said, had arrived at the US–Mexico border as unaccompanied minors. The teenagers in this case, she explained, were K’iche, the largest Indigenous Maya ethnic group in Guatemala, and like most immigrant children in the industry, they had “come with a mind [to] making money to send…back to their very poor families.”

I met with Licolli during a historic nationwide spike in child labor violations. That fiscal year, according to The Washington Post, the US labor department “found 5,792 minors working in violation of child labor laws,” an increase of 49 percent from the previous year and “an 88 percent increase since 2019.” Pete Gess, the economic policy director of Arkansas Advocates for Children & Families, noted in a 2024 report that Arkansas’s Department of Labor and Licensing had identified a 266 percent increase in child labor violations from 2020 to 2023. 

At the time I lived in downtown Little Rock, among sprawling, old, ruinous houses. Often I heard Spanish while walked down the street and looked up to see visibly underage immigrant children working on roofing crews. Sometimes I would shout up to ask them where they were from and wait for them to respond—“Guatemala” or “Mexico.” That same year Arkansas was one of eight states that made national headlines for systemic child labor violations: that February the Department of Labor found six children between the ages of thirteen and seventeen working the night shift for a third-party contractor called Packers Sanitation Services Inc. (PSSI) at a Tyson Foods plant in Green Forest, where they used harsh chemicals to clean blood, fat, bone, gristle, and skin from machines powerful enough to decapitate a worker.

Even as these violations proliferated, lawmakers in Republican-led states were taking aim at the regulations themselves. Between 2021 and 2023, fourteen states introduced or passed bills that weakened child labor laws. Two laws in particular, both passed in 2023, were at the forefront of this trend. One was in Iowa; the Economic Policy Institute (EPI), which monitors child-labor legislation, called it “one of the most dangerous rollbacks of child labor laws in the country” for, among other things, “allowing state agencies to waive restrictions on hazardous work for 16–17-year-olds in a long list of dangerous occupations.”

The other was in Arkansas. Less than a month after the Labor Department announced its findings about the Green Forest plant, Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders, who had served as Donald Trump’s press secretary during his first term, signed a bill called the Youth Hiring Act. By removing a century-old Division of Labor permission that required a parental signature for any child under sixteen seeking employment, the law effectively eliminated the only database that had kept track of working minors in the state. Sanders maintained that “all child labor laws will still apply and we expect businesses to comply just as they are required to do now.” But when I spoke to child advocates like the policy analysts Nina Mast and Reid Maki about the bill two years after it passed, both stressed that it had reduced state oversight at a time when child-labor violations were increasing.

Advertisement

Nationwide, the number of minors employed in violation of federal law remains at near-record highs. After falling to 4,030 in the 2024 fiscal year, the figure rose to 5,272 in 2025. Hazardous work violations, such as those the labor department has investigated in Arkansas’s meatpacking industry, have more than doubled since 2015, according to federal data. The state-level legislative push to dilute child-labor reporting and enforcement, meanwhile, has only gathered force. According to the EPI’s reporting, lawmakers in thirty-three states have by now introduced bills that weaken child labor laws. In 2023 Arkansas and Iowa were two of four states to successfully enact such legislation; now, three years later, fifteen states have done so. This wave of legislation may not directly affect the undocumented migrant children at the center of many recent high-profile child-labor investigations, who often take jobs via informal arrangements or under aliases, but it seems likely to discourage states from taking action to protect them and other vulnerable minors. Partly in response to these rollbacks, other legislatures have meanwhile strengthened their protections against child labor, from liberal strongholds like California and New York to red states like Texas and Alabama.

“When I started at the Wage and Hour Division in 2021,” Jessica Looman—who spent four years running the federal agency’s efforts to enforce labor laws across the country—told me in June 2025, “I did not think that by the end of 2022 our number one issue would be finding hundreds of children employed in the meatpacking industry in America.” Gess, at the Arkansas Advocates for Children & Families, stressed when we spoke in Little Rock that child labor “shouldn’t be a political issue.” In recent years, however, it has become precisely that. The rollback of child labor protections in Arkansas, I came to see, reflected a broader, increasingly politicized national campaign to weaken labor regulations, expand youth employment, and redefine the limits of hazardous and dangerous work for children.

Our current approach to regulating child labor dates back to the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) of 1938, which barred minors under eighteen from hazardous occupations. In 1941 a Georgia company, Darby Lumber, challenged the law and arrived at the Supreme Court, arguing that the states, not Congress, should have the power to regulate employment conditions. The justices, however, unanimously upheld the FLSA.

Over the past several decades Republicans have made repeated attempts to roll back child labor legislation. In 1984 President Ronald Reagan addressed Congress to propose the Youth Employment Opportunity Wage Act. “Studies over the past decade,” he insisted, “have repeatedly demonstrated that the minimum wage has reduced job opportunities for large numbers of our youth.” But lawmakers and labor organizations warned that the act would leave workers more vulnerable to exploitation, and the bill failed. In 2011 the Republican presidential candidate Newt Gingrich called child labor laws “truly stupid” and proposed putting poor children to work sweeping the floors of their classrooms: “Most of these schools ought to get rid of the unionized janitors, have one master janitor and pay local students to take care of the school.”

That same year several state legislators proposed bills to overturn youth-employment regulations. In Maine, Republicans tried to pass the “Enhance Access to Workplace for Minors” act, which would have allowed sixteen-and-seventeen-year-olds to work overnight shifts and unlimited hours on school nights, as well as lowered their wages. A limited version of the bill passed, easing restrictions on working hours. In more recent years, as Republican lawmakers and pro-business groups again began seeking to roll back child labor laws, they increasingly started speaking about defending parental and personal freedoms against government overreach.

Then, around 2020, several developments laid the groundwork for a sudden rise in child-labor violations. As Jacob Bogage and María Luisa Paúl wrote in a 2023 report for The Washington Post, the labor shortage induced by the Covid-19 pandemic “created a huge need for workers” even as “large numbers of undocumented minors entered the United States looking for work,” driven from countries such as Honduras and Guatemala by political and economic turbulence. In 2008 Congress had passed an anti-trafficking bill that included provisions preventing the Department of Homeland Security from sending back undocumented minors crossing the US–Mexico border. The intent was “to protect children who might otherwise come to harm on their own in Mexican border towns,” the journalist Hannah Dreier wrote in one of her landmark reports for The New York Times on child labor at sites including Tyson and Perdue plants. Over the following years, she noted, the policy became “widely known in Central America, where it shapes the calculations of destitute families.”

Advertisement

When the 2008 law was passed, fewer than ten thousand unaccompanied minors crossed the southern border each year. By 2014 that number had risen to 68,541; by 2021 it had risen to 144,834. During the pandemic, as Melissa Sanchez reported for ProPublica, an increasing number of immigrant teenagers started working in factories at night while attending school during the day. “Many of them passed through the federal network of shelters for unaccompanied immigrant minors that came under scrutiny in 2018 during the Trump administration’s policy of separating children from their parents,” she wrote. “As they waited weeks or months to be released to sponsors, they grew anxious about their mounting immigration debts, desperate to get out and work so their relatives back home didn’t suffer the consequences of a loan default.”

Child labor violations have risen dramatically not simply because these minors entered the country but because, once they got here, contractors were willing to exploit them to do dangerous jobs. Looman, the former Wage and Hour administrator, told me that the most frequent question people would ask her division was: “Why is child labor increasing?” In some sense, she said, “the very simple answer to that question is: because employers hired them.”

Large companies in the poultry processing industry, where child labor is especially prevalent, frequently rely on third-party contractors to fill various jobs in the supply chain. The largest of these third-party contractors is PSSI, which provides slaughterhouse cleaners and employs over 15,000 workers. (Its owner, in turn, is the private equity giant Blackstone.) By contrast, the companies that contract catchers to work at chicken houses are often small and local, and have little online presence.

Those chicken catchers, as the filmmaker Diana Campos has noted in her short documentary The Price of Poultry, work at “the bottom of the poultry industry hierarchy.” Large commercial chicken houses can hold between 30,000 and 50,000 chickens, and laborers often report working up to fifteen-hour shifts loading the birds by hand for transport to processing plants. (To work such long hours, Licolli told a local paper last December, some kids working as chicken catchers have relied on methamphetamine.) Campos was raised in Northwest Arkansas by Mexican immigrant parents; her father, who she interviews in the film, worked in the poultry industry for twenty years, including as a catcher. The people working catching shifts, she recounts partway through the documentary, “are often undocumented and sometimes children.” 

Beyond the exhausting hours, chicken catchers are at risk of serious injuries and exposed to ammonia and other hazardous chemicals, extreme heat, and respiratory illnesses. In the recent Netflix documentary Big Chicken: A Fast Food Conspiracy, the comedian Mo Gilligan interviews chicken catchers laboring under these conditions, along with advocates and journalists (including Licolli and myself). One undocumented chicken catcher shows his hands, with deformed, swollen fingers splayed in different directions. From time to time, he tells Gilligan, he loses control over them: “Sometimes when we sleep, our hands are throwing chickens.”

Catching and caging poultry are not among the seventeen hazardous occupations the Department of Labor prohibits for sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds, but the department, recognizing their risks, explicitly bans them for minors under sixteen. The sector’s layers of subcontracting and labor outsourcing, however, often obscure accountability. When Tyson and other meatpackers hire third-party providers, these providers are the first to shoulder the financial liability for employment practices and safety violations.

The Department of Labor’s findings at that Tyson plant in Green Forest were part of a months-long investigation into PSSI. Over the period in question, the department announced in February 2023, PSSI had hired more than a hundred minors to work overnight shifts at poultry plants across eight states, operated by large companies including Tyson, Cargill, and JBS; the contractor had to pay $1.5 million in civil penalties, the highest fine the government was legally able to impose. PSSI has denied knowingly hiring minors, although in the aftermath of the penalty NBC News reviewed a June 2021 PSSI report and found that the company had disciplined an employee who hired the same minor twice in six months under two different identities. In response to the fine, PSSI replaced its CEO, launched a $10 million fund to fight child labor, and, in 2025, rebranded as Fortrex.

The investigation had by then prompted some changes in compliance protocols around third-party agreements in the industry. Tyson mandated random third-party and internal audits of its sanitation partners’ hiring registries, while JBS USA canceled its contracts and started hiring its own cleaning crews. And yet allegations of child labor at Tyson persist. In 2024, according to unsealed court documents reviewed by the Arkansas Times, the Department of Labor searched a pair of the company’s plants in Arkansas after receiving anonymous tips, one from a mother who claims to have “overheard children between eleven and thirteen years old” discussing their work on the night shift in Green Forest and another from a teacher who said that one of their fourteen-year-old students talked about working at the facility in Rogers. Earlier that year, Tyson shareholders voted down a demand from Venceremos and an Arkansas faith-based organization that the company audit its plants for child labor. In 2025 the Republican Missouri senator Josh Hawley opened a congressional investigation into the company after receiving a new whistleblower complaint from a plant in an undisclosed location. “To be clear,” a Tyson spokesperson told the press in response to the Arkansas Times report, “we do not allow the employment of anyone under the age of eighteen in any of our facilities, and we do not facilitate, excuse or in any other way participate in the use of child labor.”

In June 2025 I interviewed a Tyson contractor who works at several facilities in Arkansas. (She requested anonymity for fear of retaliation.) When she first began work, she was given a tour of the plant in Springdale. “I was scared to be in there,” she told me. “And I’m an adult.” The “giant tubs where they wash the chicken” were “almost the size of my house,” she said. “There’s just an open hole. I mean, you have to climb up these stairs, a steep staircase.… And it’s water-filled with these big chickens bouncing around, almost like a washing machine.” On the production floor, she said, “It’s loud. It’s disorienting. It’s wet and slippery, and you can’t hear people talking to you. You have to wear earplugs for ear protection. But that also means that you can’t hear instructions…. A lot of people complain about headaches, a lot of chemicals going on. It’s just not a place that any child should be.”

The Arkansas Youth Hiring Act made this already opaque system still harder to regulate. When the law passed in 2023, it eliminated the requirement that children under sixteen get an employment certificate, signed by their parents, from the Arkansas Department of Labor and Licensing, which meant that the state was no longer required to verify their age. Children that age in Arkansas commonly work in fast food, bagging groceries, customer service, or seasonal work like lifeguarding; the act did not change safety or hourly protections, nor did it affect the laws that regulate hazardous jobs. It did, however, signal a rollback in state oversight of the conditions in which minors were working, precisely at a time when employers in the state were under scrutiny for child labor violations.

Sponsored by the Republican representatives Rebecca Burkes and Clint Penzo, the bill cast itself as a matter of parental rights, promising to “streamline the hiring process for children under sixteen” and “restore decision-making to parents” without government interference. Alexa Henning, Sanders’s spokesperson, echoed that language in a statement upon the signing of the bill: “the Governor believes protecting kids is most important, but this permit was an arbitrary burden on parents to get permission for their child to get a job.” When the law went through the Public Health, Welfare, and Labor Committee, according to a local news report, Burkes argued that it would give parents the freedom to dispense with the “paperwork that has to be done before the minor can accept a job.” The legislation, she noted, “came to me from the Foundation of Government Accountability [sic].”

Burkes was not the only state legislator to propose child-labor legislation from the Foundation for Government Accountability (FGA), a Florida-based think tank with a lobbying arm called FGA Action. In their Washington Post investigation of the group, Bogage and Paúl noted that the FGA had, in 2023, also helped draft several other bills, including Iowa’s; the organization, they wrote, seemed to have “found remarkable success among Republicans to relax regulations that prevent children from working long hours in dangerous conditions.” There are larger culture-war dynamics at play here: the same legislators who argue for “parental rights” when it comes to child labor have, for instance, passed laws that strip parents of the right to approve gender-affirming medical care or certain counseling for their transgender teenagers, including in Arkansas, which banned gender-affirming medical care in 2021.

After Sanders signed the Arkansas Youth Hiring Act, Nick Stehle, the FGA’s vice president of communications, wrote an op-ed for Fox News defending the law from “partisan attacks” by “out-of-state elites.” (Stehle, Burkes, and Penzo did not respond to requests for comment.) “We’re not talking about sending junior to work the graveyard shift at the factory Sunday through Saturday,” Stehle, who lives in Arkansas, wrote:

We’re talking about bussing tables a couple nights a week after school, working the check-out counter on weekends, and staying busy during summer…. The main push for this reform didn’t come from big business. It came from families like mine, who want more of the freedom that lets our children flourish.

Representative Tippi McCullough, who is serving her fourth term in the Arkansas House, voted against the bill. “I think it’s terrible,” she told me in 2025. “I don’t think it’s needed. I think, as a matter of fact, it’s harmful. I don’t think it’s pro-parental rights. I really think parents should want there to be safeguards and checks on these kinds of things.” (The New York Times opinion writer Jessica Grose made a similar point in a piece responding to the law: “Wouldn’t parents have more of a decision-making role, not less, if their explicit permission were required before their fourteen-and-fifteen-year-olds could work up to forty-eight hours a week, six days a week?”) Before serving in the House, McCullough was an English teacher and coached basketball. “I just always felt like that was a time for kids—maybe the only time in their lives—to be able to concentrate on school and extracurricular things and sports,” she said. “I mean, there’s going to be plenty of time to work the rest of your life.”

Multiple experts I spoke with argued that removing the permitting requirement would make child-labor violations harder to track. Annie B. Smith—a law professor at the University of Arkansas, where she directs the civil litigation and advocacy clinic and the human trafficking clinic—explained that “there’s less of a state role ensuring that children aren’t working, or that if they are working, they’re supposed to be working.” Debbie Berkowitz, now a fellow at Georgetown University’s Kalmanovitz Initiative for Labor and the Working Poor, served as chief of staff and then senior policy advisor for OSHA from 2009 to 2015. “What Sarah Huckabee Sanders did,” she told me in June 2025, “is allow employers to hire kids in jobs without their parents knowing, without the state knowing.”

In any case, advocates argued, safeguards for kids should rely on more than parental decision-making. “We just fundamentally feel that parents don’t know best,” Maki, the Director of Child Labor Advocacy for the National Consumers League, told me when we spoke. “They’re not looking at accident reports and poultry plants. They’re not looking at the number of kids on farms who are being dismembered or losing limbs. They just have no idea what the dangers are.” In January 2025 researchers at the University of Maryland found that states with work permit requirements had 15.5 percent fewer child-labor violation cases per million people and 35.2 percent fewer minors working under illegal conditions than states without such rules. 

That June I wrote Sam Dubke, Sanders’s communications director and speechwriter, to ask whether the governor wanted to comment on those findings and elaborate on what she was doing to prevent an increase in child labor violations in the state. “Governor Sanders takes child welfare seriously and signed legislation creating tough new civil, misdemeanor, and felony penalties for child labor violations, punishing bad actors while still giving teenagers the opportunity to learn skills in the workplace,” Dubke wrote. “All federal child labor laws are still enforced.” A month after signing the Arkansas Youth Hiring Act, Sanders did sign a bill that increased fines for child labor violations from $1,000 to $5,000 and criminalized breaking the laws knowingly. In June 2025 I emailed Steve Guntharp, the chief of staff at the Arkansas Labor Department, to confirm how many employers had been fined since the increase. The answer was two.

It was in 2023 that the Economic Policy Institute started tracking laws rolling back child labor protections across the country. “We realized this was really a much more widespread effort, legislatively, across many different states,” Mast, a policy and economic analyst at the EPI, told me, “and no one at the time was really paying that much attention to it.” In 2024, indeed, six states rolled back child labor protections. (Seven, meanwhile, passed bills that strengthened them.) According to the institute’s reporting, that year Alabama stopped requiring work permits for minors under sixteen, Florida let companies “schedule 16–17-year-olds to work more than eight hours per day on Sundays and holidays and for more than six days in a row year-round,” and Indiana rolled back protections for sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds doing hazardous agricultural work. All three bills, the EPI noted, were supported by the Foundation for Governmental Accountability. The following year West Virginia, like Arkansas, passed legislation that eliminated youth work permits for fourteen- and fifteen-year-olds; Indiana passed a law that allowed sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds to work the same hours and shifts as adults and eliminated the requirement for employers to secure written parental consent to schedule them for late shifts on school nights.

Trump has made no explicit statements about child labor since taking office, but last year, as Maki and his coauthor Todd Larsen have observed, the Trump administration “identified twenty-one offices for closure within the Labor Department’s Wage and Hour Division” and cut staff at the agency responsible for enforcing federal child labor laws. Project 2025, the Heritage Foundation’s 2023 blueprint for a second Trump term, called for watering down the Department of Labor’s hazard-order rules “to permit teenage workers access to work in regulated jobs with proper training and parental consent,” observing that “some young adults show an interest in inherently dangerous jobs.” The federal regulations have not yet been rolled back, but this past year three state legislatures—in West Virginia, Virginia, and Pennsylvania—introduced bills that would “weaken hazardous work protections for minors enrolled in work-based learning programs,” according to the EPI. West Virginia’s passed, removing the state’s specific list of hazardous occupations that were previously barred for minors under sixteen, among other things.

Trump’s immigration crackdown, too, has directly affected the landscape of child labor. The threat of deportation makes undocumented minors in the workforce more afraid than ever to report abuses, and the administration has made them still more vulnerable by systematically dismantling the legal support networks designed to help them—including by cutting funding to legal services that had long provided them with counsel.  

Elsewhere, state legislators have contemplated turning to minors to take jobs previously filled by immigrant workers. At an event in March 2025 with Tom Homan, Trump’s border tsar, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis made that connection explicit. Rather than hiring “people illegally for cheaper,” he said, “I think we’ve chosen to go a different way in Florida.” When the state passed a policy requiring many employers to verify the immigration status of their workers online, he continued, critics “said, oh, you’re not gonna be able to hire people.” But those worries, he continued, hadn’t been borne out:

Yes, we had people that left because of those rules. But you’ve also been able to hire other people—and what’s wrong with expecting, like, our young people to be working part-time now? I mean, that’s how it used to be when I was growing up. Why do we say we need to import foreigners, even import them illegally, when, you know, teenagers used to work at these resorts?

Five days after that panel discussion, a Florida state senate committee moved along a bill that would have allowed sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds to work more than eight-hour overnight shifts before the start of a school day. “It was such a bad bill,” said Maki, who noted that it was “close to getting through” before it finally died elsewhere in the Senate. The bill’s sponsor, the Tampa Republican Jay Collins, defended it during a senate debate: “Ultimately, we’re not talking about The Jungle by Upton Sinclair. We’re talking about them working at Publix, at Piggly Wiggly or jobs within the industry. This is a parental rights thing. Parents know their kids best.”

The Democratic state senator Carlos Guillermo Smith, meanwhile, spoke for the majority who voted against the legislation: “This bill is going to lead to exploitation of minors, exploitation of children.” A 2024 poll by the Florida Policy Institute showed that 74 percent of Florida voters sided with Smith against the bill, including 61 percent of Republicans and 73 percent of independents. “These leaders are kind of ignoring their own base, in some cases,” Maki said, in favor of “just pushing regressive policies on the public.”

When we spoke, Nina Mast told me that “all the organizing that has been done in opposition to these bills over the past few years” gives her hope that activists will continue fighting to keep legislators from rolling back child labor protections. In 2024 the Campaign to End US Child Labor, which represents a coalition of nearly fifty labor, human rights, and faith groups, worked with academics, survivors, and impacted communities to create a policy roadmap for local, state, and federal lawmakers. Their demands included guaranteed attorney representation for unaccompanied migrant children, the closing of loopholes in child-labor laws, “stronger consequences for child labor violations,” and the bolstering of labor rights across the board by, for instance, “raising the minimum wage, ending discrimination against farmworkers, regularizing the status of the current immigrant workforce, protecting the right to organize, and preventing states from eroding labor standards.” The National Education Association, a member of the coalition, has advocated for treating student labor exploitation as a critical threat to public education. As the Maine teacher Rie Larson put it in a 2025 NEAToday report, “Our children are not responsible for rescuing our economy.” 

Smith, the Arkansas lawyer, wishes that policymakers in Arkansas and beyond would focus on state-level interventions that address the economic needs of children and families more directly, to keep children from feeling pressured into hazardous workplaces in the first place. She also emphasized that states should pursue legislation that protects coworkers who see children doing hazardous jobs and decide to report it. Witnesses need to be able to file complaints without the risk of legal or workplace retaliation, she said, because “we know that there are simply not enough resources for the Arkansas Department of Labor or the US Department of Labor to be in every workplace.” Gess had another recommendation: finding legal pathways with which “to hold the primary company responsible for violations throughout its labor supply chain.” (Those could, for instance, be modeled on laws in other countries like Germany’s Supply Chain Act and France’s Duty of Vigilance law, both of which legally require companies to identify, prevent, and mitigate labor abuses across their global contractors.)

Many of the advocates I spoke to felt that such measures could do a good deal to help protect children like those chicken catchers that Licolli met back in 2023. But several of them also seemed unnerved by how quickly decades of consensus regarding the importance of protecting minors from hazardous work appears to be coming undone. “One hundred years ago, people started advocating to protect children because parents weren’t able to go into the workplace” and monitor conditions there, Gess told me. “Who knew a hundred years later we would be fighting some of the same battles?”

entries.title: Rachel Kushner Reads from Love and Death in the American Novel
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In this episode of Private Life, Rachel Kushner reads an excerpt from Leslie A. Fiedler’s Love and Death in the American Novel (1960), which was reissued by New York Review Books in April. In Kushner’s selection, Fiedler writes about Mark Twain and the themes and characters of his books The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876) and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884).

Kushner is best known for her novels Telex from Cuba (2008), The Flamethrowers (2013), and The Mars Room (2018). Her most recent novel is Creation Lake (2024).

Leslie A. Fiedler (1917–2003) was a literary critic and novelist. His books include The Stranger in Shakespeare (1972), Freaks: Myths and Images of the Secret Self (1978), and Fiedler on the Roof: Essays on Literature and Jewish Identity (1991).

Last week’s episode featured Edwin Frank in a conversation about Fiedler’s literary criticism and Love and Death in the American Novel. You can find Love and Death in the American Novel at nyrb.com or at your favorite bookseller.

entries.title: Jefferson, Independence, and Slavery
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In the first episode of Endgame with Fintan O’Toole, the Review’s newest podcast, O’Toole welcomes Annette Gordon-Reed, author of the Pulitzer Prize–winning history The Hemingses of Monticello, for a conversation about Thomas Jefferson, the legacy of slavery in the United States, the original preamble to the Declaration of Independence, and the fate of the Voting Rights Act.

Annette Gordon-Reed has been a frequent contributor to The New York Review for the last ten years. Her Pulitzer Prize–winning The Hemingses of Monticello: An American Family revised our understanding of Thomas Jefferson’s relationship with Sally Hemings, and for the Review she has written about subjects ranging from W.E.B. Du Bois to Hillary Clinton to the history of Texas. She is the Carl M. Loeb University Professor at Harvard. Her latest book is Jefferson on Race: A Reader.

New episodes from Endgame’s first season will appear every Tuesday, and will be available on all major podcast platforms. Visit here to subscribe.

entries.title: The Dream of AI Primacy
entries.summary: The US drive to win the AI race against China now feeds a fantasy of permanent American dominance in global affairs.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
At a White House state dinner, proximity to the president is a measure of power—or at least of favor. At the glittering banquet for the Chinese leader Xi Jinping on September 24, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang sat directly across from Donald Trump. The companies represented at their table were worth nearly $15 trillion. OpenAI’s Sam Altman was seated within spitting distance of his longtime antagonist Elon Musk. Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg was also on the guest list. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who had repeatedly sparred with the administration before a recent rapprochement, was not.

China looms over these men’s visions of the AI future, but they disagree sharply about it. For Amodei, whose firm has warned that AI may pose an “existential risk to humanity,” the prospect of Chinese advances is a source of dread. He has warned publicly that Chinese AI projects not only risk slipping out of human control but could also enable autocracies, led by China, to achieve “permanent military superiority” over the United States and its democratic allies.

Amodei hopes that getting ahead now could allow the US to prevent anyone from ever catching up. He has held out the dream of an “eternal 1991”: the West’s moment of triumph at the end of the cold war extended indefinitely by AI. In this vision, democracies would “parlay their AI superiority into a durable advantage.” When Amodei recently called for slowing the pace of AI development and exploring cooperation with China, he cautioned that any American slowdown should be “limited by the lead that US companies have” over China.

Although Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent opposes a pause on AI development, he agrees with Amodei on the near-apocalyptic stakes regarding China: “There is no day after tomorrow if China wins at this.” Nvidia’s Huang, a skeptic of catastrophic AI warnings and a staunch ally of Trump’s, disagrees. When the CNN anchor Fareed Zakaria asked him if it matters whether the United States or China wins the AI race, he said, “I don’t think it does.”

From Beijing’s perspective, disagreements among these tech titans matter less than the American power they collectively represent. Before Xi’s visit to Washington, Chinese state media launched a stunning attack on Anthropic that described the firm as emblematic of the United States itself. The polemic called Anthropic “entirely a monster bred by the American path” in pursuit of “technological hegemony.” Many Chinese AI experts I spoke with interpreted recent American calls for an AI slowdown as an effort to slow China down and trap it in second place.

Beijing recognizes a strand of American thinking that has received too little attention in the US: the conviction that advanced AI may bring the return of American global primacy. In his influential 2024 essay “Situational Awareness,” the technology investor Leopold Aschenbrenner predicted the rapid arrival of superintelligence. “Those who have it will wield complete dominance over those who don’t,” he wrote, urging America to secure absolute AI preeminence over China. In 2024 Amodei was asked about the essay and acknowledged, “My view is, I would say, not particularly far from it.” (Aschenbrenner’s essay was closely read by officials in the Biden administration, where Amodei was particularly influential, and found an even more unlikely fan in Ivanka Trump, who called it “an excellent and important read.”)

Twentieth-century visions of American primacy rested on overwhelming military and economic power, but the new AI primacists imagine something more drastic: a winner-take-all technology that could allow American power to increase faster than rivals can catch up, making its primacy permanent. Call this “recursive advantage.” Recursive self-improvement is a feedback loop in which AI systems help build increasingly capable successors, potentially with diminishing human involvement. Historically, technological diffusion allowed developing countries to gradually narrow gaps with more powerful rivals. In the primacists’ vision, AI would break this catch-up mechanism, allowing the leading country to accelerate innovation and deny rivals the means to close the gap.

It is a long leap from building a smarter machine to securing lasting command of world affairs. There are strong reasons to maintain the US lead in developing and deploying AI and to use export controls to prevent advanced American technology from empowering China’s military or apparatus of repression.* A lead can bring substantial economic, scientific, and military benefits. For this reason, Chinese firms are racing to match American advances, and Xi has positioned technologies like AI as the “main battlefield of international competition.” A lead could also help Washington negotiate meaningful global AI rules and safeguards from a position of strength. But securing these benefits of staying ahead does not require an absolute and permanent monopoly.

The primacist vision is remarkably imprecise on fundamental questions. Why would accelerated AI research benefit only the leader? What would prevent diffusion, espionage, independent discovery, or rival powers from disrupting that lead? (Indeed, China’s AI models have already made advances that shocked many observers.) Would an advantage possessed by an American company reliably become power controlled by—or at least put in service of—the American state? Nor is there a clear test for when the race has been “won” or a reliable way to identify in advance the thresholds beyond which humans could lose control. The promise of eventual supremacy has become a rationale for accepting mounting risks along the way. Even signs of danger can become arguments to accelerate; by this reasoning, only stronger AI-enabled defenses can protect against increasingly dangerous AI-powered attacks.

Advertisement

To be sure, not every Silicon Valley leader believes in the notion of recursive advantage. Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind has suggested that AI progress may be more incremental than this “hard-takeoff” scenario suggests. Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, the AI executive Alexandr Wang, and the researcher Dan Hendrycks have warned that pursuing a “strategic monopoly on power” through AI—making the country that possesses it “as overwhelming as the Conquistadors were to the Aztecs”—could provoke uncontrolled escalation or outright war.

Other companies, such as Meta and Microsoft, describe a vision of American power based on spreading American AI infrastructure globally (which they hope to profit from propagating) in competition with Chinese systems, rather than on technological supremacy alone. These arguments suggest that the global diffusion of open-weight Chinese models, which are cheap or free and can be easily modified by their users, may be a strategic blind spot for many in Washington. Building the most advanced models does not guarantee influence over how the world uses AI.

Some who argue for absolute US dominance believe that achieving it would be stabilizing and is necessary to control the technology’s risks, allowing a responsible America to impose safety standards on a reckless world. But Trump’s America has hardly shown itself to be responsible, and the Trump administration has so far opposed efforts to regulate AI. (A “White House Accord on Super Intelligence” signed on September 29 by Trump, Musk, Amodei, Huang, Zuckerberg, and others took a lowest-common-denominator position, endorsing voluntary internal controls and external audits at each company while deferring regulation.) In any event, a mistrustful Beijing would fiercely resist unilaterally imposed American safety standards, as would the US if the positions were reversed. Making China’s irreversible subordination the goal gives Beijing every reason to suspect that any offer of restraint is a demand for surrender.

This winner-take-all vision is influential among both Republican and Democratic elites, but the American public appears far less willing to subordinate safety to promises of global primacy. In a survey from early September, 69 percent of respondents believed that the US government should pass strong AI rules right away to protect workers and prevent dangerous outcomes, even if they slowed America’s AI development. Only 14 percent believed that the government should hold back on major regulation so that US companies could stay ahead of China. A recent global Gallup poll showed that only 36 percent of Americans who were aware of AI believed it would “mostly help” people in their country—putting the US in the bottom five countries globally for AI optimism.

Chinese people, by contrast, appear more sanguine. The same Gallup poll showed that 93 percent of respondents in China believed that AI will “mostly help” people in their country. The Chinese government has introduced AI regulations still largely absent in the United States, from labeling AI-generated content to issuing child safety guidelines. When Chinese Communist Party leaders speak of the need for AI to remain “secure and controllable,” they emphasize protecting the regime’s control and extending the tools of surveillance, repression, and digital authoritarianism that they have been perfecting since the advent of the Internet. Chinese AI experts have begun to discuss what one regulator called “extreme loss of control” scenarios, but Beijing has not yet experienced an explosion of concern about existential AI risk comparable to the responses to Jacob Coxon’s resignation from Anthropic in September. Greater concern about its own vulnerability to those risks could eventually give Beijing a stronger incentive to constrain AI development, even at some cost to its pursuit of advanced capabilities.

Yet Beijing need not embrace the theory of recursive advantage to react to it. Whether Chinese leaders seek permanent superiority themselves or fear that Washington could achieve it, the prospect adds to the pressure to accelerate AI development. If restraint appears to mean permanent subordination, continuing the race could seem less dangerous—even if their concern about AI catastrophe grows.

Abandoning the ambition for primacy would not make Beijing a trustworthy partner or ensure its willingness to accept verifiable limits. But the pursuit of permanent dominance appears to lack American public support and makes cooperation even less likely precisely when it is becoming more necessary.

Advertisement

Each week brings fresh evidence that AI companies can lose control over the systems they are building: autonomous OpenAI agents have accessed government websites, leaked user data, and bypassed constraints to hack external servers. Bessent has announced an open line of communication with his Chinese counterpart on AI. Yet neither government appears ready to limit the pace of AI development or to engage in serious diplomacy about the risks.

Xi’s visit to Washington was a missed opportunity on this score. Rather than start a meaningful discussion of AI, as the two sides had suggested might occur before the summit, Trump used the occasion to press for agreement on a new name for it: “Super Intelligence,” or SI. “He likes the idea of changing the name to SI, too,” Trump declared proudly after Xi departed town. The Chinese readouts from the summit continued to call it AI.

Trump has made clear that he has no intention of slowing down, nor does he expect China to do so. “The United States of America is not going to be putting on brakes,” he said after the meeting. A race driven by the prospect of permanent supremacy could unleash forces neither country can control. Both Trump and Xi would do well to remember that even race cars have brakes.

—October 7, 2026

  • *

    See my “When the Chips Are Down,” The New York Review, February 26, 2026. ↩

entries.title: Our 1989
entries.summary: On October 7, 1989, East Germany celebrated its fortieth anniversary with a military parade down Karl-Marx-Allee—an old-fashioned display of state power as protests against Communist rule spread across the country. entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
On October 7, 1989, East Germany celebrated its fortieth anniversary with a military parade down Karl-Marx-Allee—an old-fashioned display of state power as protests against Communist rule spread across the country. Opponents of the regime were galled by the phalanxes of goose-stepping soldiers and columns of tanks. That same day, representatives of East Berlin’s theaters gathered secretly in the side foyer of the Volksbühne, which had opened in 1914 as part of a socialist effort to break the upper-class monopoly on education and the arts.

Built in a rounded, modernist style, the Volksbühne famously promoted a program of “Art to the People,” a sentiment that should have been in line with the country’s ideals. Instead it was in this theater for the people that opposition against the people’s government coalesced, helping to lead to the huge November 4 demonstration on Alexanderplatz, when hundreds of thousands turned out to demand change. Hanging over the protests was the possibility of a “Chinese solution,” as people at the time put it: the East German government had supported Beijing’s bloody suppression of the Tiananmen demonstrations that June, and many feared it might respond similarly at home.

But events unfolded more peacefully. Under pressure from the Soviet Union to begin bold reforms, East Berlin’s leaders were reluctant to unleash their security forces, especially after the international outcry over the Tiananmen massacre. And so just five days after the huge protests the Berlin Wall was opened, and a few months later the country’s first free election resulted in a win for parties that promised speedy reunification with West Germany. Less than a year after the meeting in the Volksbühne, East Germany ceased to exist. These events helped create the Western legend of 1989 as a turning point when freedom and democracy suddenly seemed to be spreading around the globe.

Thirty-seven years later the Volksbühne is returning to the events of 1989, this time in the form of a coproduction with the influential Berlin-based theater collective Rimini Protokoll. The result is House of Hopes, an ambitious production that tells intersecting stories of how that year played out around the world. The production builds on Rimini Protokoll’s longstanding practice of having nonprofessional performers—“experts of the everyday”—tell their own stories to audiences in immersive, unorthodox theatrical settings. Earlier works, such as 100% City and Situation Rooms, used that method to explore demography and the global arms trade; House of Hopes turns it toward historical memory, allowing personal experiences of the same year to coexist and collide.

Set in ten countries—Afghanistan, Chile, China, Hungary, Japan, Namibia, Poland, Romania, South Korea, and the United States—the stories complicate the conventional Western narrative of 1989. The most obvious counterpoint to Berlin is Beijing, but the year was critical in many other countries as well, often in unexpected or indirect ways. The Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan preceded civil war and eventually Taliban rule; South Korea’s democratization left the chaebol with enormous economic influence; Namibia was casting off South African rule, but one party has ruled the country ever since; some of the leaders of the opposition to Communist rule that year in Hungary and Poland later embraced right-wing nationalism (a historical twist that resonated strongly during the performance with the rise of the far-right AfD party in Germany). The stories aren’t meant merely as excuses to relive that heady moment or as exercises in historical revisionism but rather as new vantage points from which to see our post–cold war world.

At the start of each staging of House of Hopes, organizers divide the audience randomly into ten groups. Each of those groups experiences seven of the stories, which the cast performs in different parts of the theater: the foyer, stage, wings, balconies. (The Volksbühne calls it a Hausbegehung, or a walk-through of the building.) Each story lasts about fifteen minutes before the groups set off to find their next location. Often they can see one another, but they wear headphones that isolate each narrator’s story.

Rimini Protokoll’s trick is to make these histories something more than testimony. Again and again spectators find themselves enlisted in someone else’s past, directed to take part in that performance—often without understanding how their actions will appear from elsewhere in the building. On the night I attended I heard a Chilean woman explain that she participated in protests against Augusto Pinochet’s dictatorship, which in 1989 resulted in a series of laws that codified the country’s return to democracy. She invited us to imitate her gestures, for example by shaking our fists in the air. At the same time, down by the stage, the Afghan narrator told his group to turn around and watch us—an unruly crowd, he said, threatening impending violence.

The autobiographical stories have a certain bittersweet humor. The Hungarian storyteller told of growing up in the period after the 1956 uprising, a failure that scarred the country for decades. After 1989 her parents decided to go into business and had to decide what would sell well in the turbulent 1990s. With crime rising, they hit upon the idea of car alarms—and so the family home became a store, with a workshop in the basement, office staff on the second floor, and the tasks of daily life sandwiched in between. The audience recreated the soundtrack of her childhood, shaking keyrings, clicking analog phones, and rustling papers to a beat she conducted. Looking back, she was amazed at her parents’ ability to survive but glad she didn’t have to muster the same resourcefulness: “Unlike my parents, I didn’t have to adapt; I could leave.”

Advertisement

The narrator of the Iranian story stood in the foyer in front of a giant collage of photos: arid mountains, fighter jets, ancient stone sculptures, dictators, mullahs, childhood fun, and Bollywood films. Growing up under Ayatollah Khomeini’s rule, she remembered, she returned repeatedly to one action-adventure film in particular, the Hindi megahit Sholay, watching it so often that she memorized the dance sequences. She was mostly fatherless, because her dad had been arrested for shaving his beard and was only released in order to serve on the front after Iraq invaded Iran. In 1989 Khomeini died, filling much of the country with “omid,” hope for change.

That hope was dashed, and the speaker, like most of the performers, went abroad. She told us that she calls home often, with her mother offering her one piece of advice: keep dancing. Then the woman left the foyer for a few moments until a man walked up to the collage and pulled it back—it was only a curtain, and behind it was a bank of windows opening onto the dark streets of Berlin. A narrow spotlight lit the woman out on the street as she danced the Sholay choreography from her childhood.

By then another pattern had emerged. Many of these accounts are also stories of diaspora: memories of a time and place that cannot be recovered, recounted by people who now find themselves in Berlin. The Iranian performer’s childhood dance made that displacement almost literal.

Nowhere did the distance between past and present feel more consequential than in the story of Beijing’s 1989. The speaker had spent much of her life inside the system whose history she was about to describe. Growing up during the Cultural Revolution, she and millions of other young people from the cities were sent to the countryside to labor with the peasants. After Mao’s death she returned to the city, studied, and eventually landed a job in the central government.

When the student-led protests began in the spring of 1989, she regularly walked over to watch the demonstrations and soak in the atmosphere. One of her relatives was a hunger-striker on Tiananmen Square, where she visited him. Behind her a huge screen displayed the interior of the Great Hall of the People, the monumental structure on the square that serves as one of the symbolic centers of Chinese state power. As she talked, other images slowly appeared overlaid onto it: photos of demonstrators and banners calling for democracy.

“We begin to dream. Some want the leaders to step down. Our dream did not come true.”

The screen suddenly turned white.

“You can find pictures of what happened on Tiananmen on the Internet, but I can’t show it.”

When she returned to her government work she was criticized for attending the protests, even if she was mainly an observer. She wrote self-criticisms for months and finally checked herself into a clinic to escape the pressure. “Many leave China,” she went on.

But I don’t run away. I stay. I still believe that our economic reforms can help the people. Ten years later I lose my hope, and I quit my job. The economy booms but not democracy.

You may wonder what happened to my relative, the one who was a hunger-striker on Tiananmen Square. He became a top manager at a computer company. He’s very rich now and doesn’t talk about what happened on the square. And I can only talk about it here under a fake name.

entries.title: Between Earth and Sky
entries.summary: Oleksandr Dovzhenko was a connoisseur of clouds. In many of his shots, the big sky of Ukraine’s fields and steppe swallows the frame. entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Oleksandr Dovzhenko was a connoisseur of clouds. In many of his shots, the big sky of Ukraine’s fields and steppe swallows the frame. When tiny human forms emerge upward into the heavens, they come as a surprise. As they grow they become monumental, often viewed from below. This is a fairly standard technique in Soviet visual art, which had a mandate to make workers look like heroes. But Dovzhenko goes a step further by making his characters look less like statues than like natural features, the wrinkles on their faces as noble as riverbeds.

Earth (1930), Dovzhenko’s silent masterpiece, is not only a celebration of agricultural collectivization—a predictable assignment for a filmmaker working at a Soviet studio—but an ode to the cycles of life, which resist the linear logic of Stalinist industrialization. In the opening scene, an old man eats a pear, smiles, and expires under a fruit tree; a beautiful death. His grandson Vasyl, a strapping young peasant, the hero of the collectivization effort, brings in the village’s first tractor to great fanfare, but it stalls on the road. He and his friends solve the problem of an overheated radiator by taking turns pissing into it. Dovzhenko films cows and horses as if they are people; with the rest of the villagers, they watch the march of progress with curiosity and trepidation. In real life millions of peasants were deported, executed, or starved during collectivization. Many animals died too, killed by owners who refused to see them confiscated by the state.

Vasyl is murdered by a “kulak” who doesn’t want to give up his land. The hero’s body is carried past an orchard whose branches brush his cheeks, past a field of sunflowers. His mother gives birth while he is being buried. Luminous rain pours over the village’s fruit trees and his girlfriend finds happiness in the arms of another man. Life goes on. The sunflowers that figure so prominently in Earth are now one of Ukraine’s national symbols; the flag is blue for the sky and gold for the fields.

Dovzhenko—subject of “Earth and Empire,” a new retrospective at Metrograph—is Ukraine’s most famous director, but he’s a complicated hero for a Ukraine at war with Russia. (The film studio named for him in Kyiv was hit by Russian strikes in June.) His films are mind-bogglingly beautiful paeans to Ukraine’s land and its people, animals, and plants, but he also played the Soviet game, his work vetted and reviewed by state organs and censors. He likely survived the 1930s only thanks to Stalin’s personal patronage and protection. Ukraine’s greatest director hid his youthful affiliation with Ukrainian nationalism, embraced Bolshevism, and created magnificent works exalting the October Revolution and the collectivization of agriculture, two of the most traumatic moments in Ukraine’s twentieth-century history. His films celebrate the Communist project, but at their best they depict human suffering and survival with a complexity that is alien to propaganda.

Born to Ukrainian peasants in a village in Chernigov region in 1894, Dovzhenko was the seventh of fourteen children. Rampant epidemics (typhoid, typhus) meant that by the time he was eleven, according to his biographer George Liber, he was the oldest living sibling in the family.1 Though his parents were illiterate, he went to school and trained as a teacher. He escaped enlistment in World War I, but he does seem to have served in the army of the nationalist leader Symon Petlyura’s short-lived Ukrainian People’s Republic during the tumultuous period between 1917 and 1919, when the Cheka arrested him at the border between Ukraine and Poland. His sentence for fighting under Petlyura was apparently reversed by the Borotbists, Ukrainian peasant communists, leading to his release; two years later he started working as a diplomat representing the Ukrainian Socialist Soviet Republic. The reversal of his fortunes remains a mystery. In his 1939 autobiography he simply claimed that he served as a Red Army schoolteacher from 1918 to 1920—the most appropriate lie, affirming his support for the Bolsheviks from the beginning and downplaying his history of association with the Ukrainian independence movement. He also spent a short period in Germany, where he befriended the painter George Grosz.

From then on Dovzhenko was an artist. He worked as a caricaturist before starting work as a film director at the Odesa Film Factory. After a few unexceptional films, in 1928 he completed Zvenygora. The magical-Bolshevik historical epic was recognized immediately as an extraordinary breakthrough, though it would soon fade from view, revived only after Khrushchev’s Thaw in the 1950s. “Zvenygora leaps!,” Sergei Eisenstein wrote after seeing an early screening in Moscow. Arsenal, about the revolution in Ukraine, followed in 1929, and Earth came the following year. Together the three films comprise Dovzhenko’s so-called “Ukrainian trilogy.” As the scholar Roman Rosliak has shown, Dovzhenko was under police surveillance beginning in the late 1920s, when he and a group of Ukrainians at the Odesa Film Factory tried to form their own professional association.2 The surveillance continued until his death in 1956. As he made his masterpieces, his colleagues and friends were coerced into informing the secret police about his complaints and aspirations. When the secret police called, it was almost impossible to refuse them.

Advertisement

Zvenygora takes its premise from an old folk tale in which a peasant discovers a treasure in a cave. When he takes only two coins, he prospers. But when he returns for more he finds the cave filled with snakes. The wind tells him to take only what he needs. In Dovzhenko’s hands the old story becomes a cinematic poem about Ukraine’s buried riches, updated with Soviet politics and avant-garde aesthetics. Cossacks gallop out of the forest in slow motion; they are hunting for liakhs, a name for western Slavs, who are searching for the buried treasure. We meet the “mossy old man” who has guarded the hoard for centuries; he leads the Cossacks to Zvenygora, the mountain where the treasure is hidden. The Cossacks shoot the liakhs out of the trees and laugh raucously as the bodies tumble to the ground, the foliage rustling. (“A liakh sat in an oak tree,” an intertitle tells us in the sardonic-folkloric register of the film. “And the liakh was no more.”) When a Cossack and the old man pounce on a silver goblet in the grass, it becomes a clouded, broken glass.

A better future is embodied here, as in all the films in Dovzhenko’s Ukrainian trilogy, by the robust, square-jawed young actor Semyon Svashenko, who plays Timosha, one of the old man’s two grandsons. (Offscreen, Svashenko’s brother was a writer killed in 1937, one of many Ukrainian-language writers purged under Stalin.) Rather than dreaming of gold, Timosha works hard in his village, fixing machinery. The other grandson finds work in Paris, earning money by tricking decadent theatergoers into believing he will shoot himself on stage. “Ladies and gentlemen! I am very grateful for your attention,” he tells them. “I know that you are not interested in either Ukraine or in the Bolsheviks…” He keeps talking, but we don’t know what he says. The onlookers pant with excitement. He raises the revolver, then pauses and keeps talking, buying time until a policeman, his accomplice, pulls him off stage.

He is, it turns out, raising funds to help him search for the buried treasure. Back in Ukraine he persuades his grandfather to sabotage the train that’s being built over the supposed cache. He is an enemy of progress, of the future. He has faith in neither the Bolsheviks nor Ukraine. But Timosha stops the sabotage and rescues his grandfather from being run over. The film’s last shot is of a train speeding forward: an easy metaphor for progress, but with a threatening undertone. What lay ahead for Ukraine, though Dovzhenko didn’t know it, were cataclysmic artificial famines and several more devastating wars, corrupt politicians using Ukraine’s survival as a bargaining chip, and long, fruitless rumors of hidden treasure.

Dovzhenko benefited from the “Ukrainianization” of the 1920s, part of a larger Soviet project to cultivate distinct cultural and linguistic identities in the non-Russian Soviet Socialist Republics and among recognized minorities. Ukrainian filmmakers were encouraged to pursue distinctly Ukrainian themes, an enticing prospect for Dovzhenko, with his passion for the Ukrainian countryside and his past flirtations with Ukrainian nationalism. Zvenygora doubles as a chronicle of Ukrainian history, from the days of the Scythians to the Cossacks to World War I, when village happiness is shattered by conscription. Men march off to the sound of accordions; women cry.

Timosha joins the Bolsheviks. His girlfriend begs him not to ride off, telling him to kill her if he won’t return to the village. He points his gun at her and we see her shadow crumple to the ground—but we don’t see her body. Dovzhenko consistently averts the gaze of the camera when it seems that someone is about to be killed. At first this seems like tact. Dovzhenko, after all, was finely attuned to suffering and death, something he had lived with since childhood and experienced on an ever-greater scale as he witnessed World War I, revolution, civil war, and collectivization. “Whenever I think of my childhood and of my home, in my mind I see crying and funerals,” he wrote. “I still cannot bear to look at funerals, and yet they pass through all my scripts and all my pictures, for the question of life and death affected my imagination when I was still a child and left its imprint on all my work.” After these scenes where the camera looks away, we sometimes learn that the person wasn’t killed at all. In Dovzhenko’s universe, suffering is near-constant, but death, like treasure, can be a metaphor or a matter of debate.

Advertisement

Arsenal, a darkly dazzling portrait of Ukraine after the October Revolution and during the civil war that followed, has a newly painful resonance at a time when central Kyiv is struck by Russian missiles almost daily. A painterly scene of peasant women with downturned faces is brought into motion by a one-legged man swinging across the street on crutches, a child following him. “There was a war,” the intertitles tell us tersely, and it is impossible not to think of the tens of thousands of Ukrainians, mostly men but women too, who have lost limbs to Russian weapons. The cruelty of bad rulers trickles down; a miserable mother beats her crying child in a rhythmic pulse, and a man with one arm beats a starving horse. Then Dovzhenko gives the horse—a descendent of the Christ-like horses of Tolstoy and Dostoevsky—an intertitle of its own, admonishing the man for beating it.

We get lost in the intricacies of the civil war, but are rescued by Semyon Svashenko, again called Timosha. His travels allow Dovzhenko to create scenes evoking the many strains of nationalist thought in Ukraine at the time. Priests march before a painting of Taras Shevchenko, the poet and former serf who became Ukraine’s national bard, carrying it at a gathering of believers in front of St. Sophia Cathedral in central Kyiv. We see another painting of Shevchenko in a private home, where a man lights a candle and puts it under the icon. Suddenly Shevchenko moves his eyes and turns his head; the icon has come alive.3

Moments like these, along with all the other slants and caesuras in Dovzhenko’s work, not only advance his films into the realm of the sublime but give them a level of political and moral ambiguity that was rare in Soviet film, if not in the small subsection of Soviet masterpieces that are still watched and celebrated today. Timosha, when asked if he is Ukrainian, says “I am a worker,” frowns with deep thought, and then confirms, “Yes, a worker.” Like Dovzhenko, he seems torn between his identities as a Bolshevik worker-revolutionary and a Ukrainian peasant eager for liberation. Dovzhenko never stopped identifying as a Ukrainian. But there was an exceedingly fine, wavering line, for a Soviet Ukrainian director, between making politically palatable films about Ukraine and evincing a level of solidarity with other Ukrainians that could brand him as a nationalist—a charge that could mean death.

In Arsenal the revolution is represented not as a triumph but as a series of bereaved women, of grim executions. At the end of the film, Timosha is caught by Ukrainian nationalist soldiers who shout “Stop! Who are you?” “A Ukrainian worker,” he answers, finding the union of the two identities. “Shoot!” They fire at him, but he doesn’t fall. When they ask if he’s wearing armor, he bares his chest, miraculously unharmed. The film ends there, with the Ukrainian worker-revolutionary defiant, immortal but also vulnerable. As the critic Gilberto Perez wrote, “Arsenal is singular among Soviet films in the way it combines, without diluting either thesis or antithesis in this central contradiction, a militant advocacy of revolution and a dolorous sense of its tragedy.”

In Zvenygora, we come to understand that the treasure is not a cache of Cossack gold but Ukraine’s natural resources: its black earth, its mountains, its forests and rivers. But who does it belong to? Here, too, Dovzhenko’s films now suggest not only veiled criticisms of Stalinist policies that starved the Ukrainian countryside to feed the cities, but also premonitions of Hitler’s dream of using Ukraine’s black earth to feed German expansion, Russia’s attempt to reclaim Ukraine’s industrial east, and even Trump’s efforts to make deals for Ukraine’s mineral resources. We might think, also, of recent episodes when rivers, swamps, and forests have helped fend off Russian invasion.

Soviet debates about the appropriate use of natural resources often referred to nature’s “treasure,” from buried minerals to the rivers that powered the hydroelectric dams so central to Soviet industrialization and thus to Soviet art. Dovzhenko’s first sound film, Ivan (1932), is about a Ukrainian peasant transformed by participation in the construction of the Dnieper Hydroelectric Station, in what is now Zaporizhzhia. Destroyed during World War II to impede the German advance, the station was later rebuilt, but stopped generating power in 2024 after being hit by a Russian missile. In Ivan huge expanses of water, first serene and then tumultuous, match the expanses of sky. The stillness of the landscape is broken suddenly by the chaos and violence of construction. Ivan is a continuation of the projects of Arsenal and Earth, a formally inventive portrait of industrialization that shows at least some of the violence and death caused by the process, while also making clear the beauty not only of the Ukrainian landscape but also of the dream of modernization.

Ivan was intensely criticized in Ukraine for both ideological and artistic failures, at a time when bad reviews could mean ostracism, deportation, arrest, or even death. The hero was not heroic enough; the villain was too sympathetic; the Ukrainian landscape was portrayed with too much longing; the peasants seemed helpless in the face of the construction project. The Soviet Ukrainian Politburo denounced those involved with Ivan for “political blindness.” Dovzhenko and his wife Yuliya Solntseva, a Russian film star best known for playing the Martian queen Aelita, escaped to Moscow, where Dovzhenko met Stalin, an avid cinephile as well as a failed poet in his youth. Stalin liked Ivan very much, and soon Ukrainian critics did, too.

Dovzhenko’s next film was Aerograd (1935), about the construction of a new city in the far eastern Siberian taiga. (We never see the city.) The sea of trees matches the vastness of the sky, which is the poetic equivalent of the future; the aerial scenes are astonishing. The film is marred, however, by the cartoonish rivalry between the heroes and the Japanese warriors and Old Believers who try to stop them in their mission. Aerograd, despite its poetry, is the moment when Dovzhenko’s work began to slip into the realm of true propaganda.

Before long Stalin tapped Dovzhenko to make a biopic of Mykola Shchors, a Ukrainian Bolshevik military hero who had died in 1919 and therefore never had a chance to be purged. Despite Stalin’s patronage, the filming of Shchors was beset with difficulties both practical and ideological. The commander of Kharkiv Military District, a crucial character in the film, was arrested during filming, meaning that the scenes featuring him had to be thrown out and the script revised. Dovzhenko spent three months bedridden with coronary disease. Enemies seemed to surround him. In 1938, Rosliak notes, someone sabotaged his car and he almost died in a crash. A gun on the set of Shchors was found to be loaded with a real bullet.

Against all odds, this film was the greatest success—in a nonartistic sense—of Dovzhenko’s career; it won him a Stalin Prize. Perhaps Stalin had marked Dovzhenko for survival, as he sometimes did with favored artists. Dovzhenko’s luck seemed to run out in 1944, when Stalin read his screenplay for a World War II film, Ukraine in Flames, and accused him of nationalism, revisions of Leninism, and more: Dovzhenko had made a misstep by depicting the failures of the Soviet resistance to the Nazi invasion and by showing Ukrainians uniting in the struggle against Hitler. According to the prevailing line, Soviet citizens were all equivalent, whether Russian, Ukrainian, or Jewish. Dovzhenko’s rendering was taken as a dangerous sign of Ukrainian nationalism, an especially grave charge after Ukrainian nationalists’ wartime alliance with the Nazis. But Dovzhenko survived.

When Dovzhenko died in 1956—the year of Khrushchev’s “Secret Speech,” which prompted the de-Stalinization of the USSR—he was about to begin filming Poem of the Sea, about villagers saying good-bye to their home before it is submerged by the construction of the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Dam near Kherson, the final dam in the Dnieper reservoir cascade. Solntseva, his widow and frequent assistant director, agreed to direct the film in his stead. (She was assisted by Dovzhenko’s student Larisa Shepitko, soon to emerge as one of the USSR’s most brilliant filmmakers and an heir to Dovzhenko.) Poem of the Sea is touching, but it has a certain midcentury Soviet woodenness and feels shockingly conventional compared to Dovzhenko’s work. For years largely forgotten, it gained new currency after the Kakhovka Dam was blown up in 2023, presumably by Russian forces, flooding forty towns and villages, killing livestock, and washing huge quantities of toxins into the Black Sea. Residents of the region testify to their grief in poignant comments on the film posted on YouTube.

Solntseva directed two more films based on Dovzhenko’s scripts: The Tale of Fiery Years (1961), a revised version of Ukraine in Flames, and The Enchanted Desna (1964), based on Dovzhenko’s autobiographical “film tale” of the same name, a lyrical account of the landscapes, both internal and external, of his childhood. Jean-Luc Godard listed The Enchanted Desna as his favorite film of 1965; its child’s perspective and focus on consciousness rather than narrative give it an obvious nouvelle vague appeal. And with its folkloric modernism in brilliant color, its rustic dreamscapes pierced by sudden violence, The Enchanted Desna also has something in common with Sergei Paradjanov’s psychedelic poem of the Carpathians, Shadows of Forgotten Ancestors (1965). Solntseva made the most of the enormous progress in sound engineering since Dovzhenko began making talkies with Ivan; the film’s voluptuous surround sound embraces the viewer with the music of the Ukrainian countryside. In the voiceover we seem to hear Dovzhenko’s voice from beyond the grave. He recalls how, as a child, he felt that if he could harness just a thousandth of the sky’s clouds and arrange them in books or paintings, his life would not have been in vain.

Solntseva at first received little credit for her work on the films, which were seen as posthumous Dovzhenko releases, but since then her reputation has been revived by film critics who see her as an important figure in her own right. In Ukraine some critics have denounced her, without much evidence, as an NKVD informant who surveilled and even manipulated Dovzhenko on the orders of her handler—according to one story, she reported that Dovzhenko spoke Ukrainian in his sleep—or as a Russian who sought to tear Dovzhenko away from Ukraine. The loving depictions of Ukraine in The Enchanted Desna make this latter charge seem rather ludicrous.

Dovzhenko liked to leave important dialogue to our imagination, omitting intertitles at moments that seem pivotal. His characters are often gazing at some mysterious object outside the frame. The ambiguity of his best films presents a complicated challenge for the composers who score them. Metrograph’s screenings of the Ukraine trilogy will be accompanied by new, live scores by musicians who are well aware of everything that has happened in Ukraine in the century since Dovzhenko began his career: the pianist Fima Chupakhin, the bandurist Julian Kystasty, and the band medukha, which describes its work as “Slavic folk songs steeped in psych-rock sensibilities.” Medukha’s score will include accordion, electric guitar, guzheng, and viola, a cosmopolitan blend of old and new, folkloric and avant-garde, that suits Dovzhenko well.

It will be fascinating to see how Dovzhenko’s films, with their wide-open spaces, reinvent themselves in the company of these new songs. That said, I watched Arsenal on a screener that had no musical accompaniment, and I appreciated the silence; it made me feel the interstices and ambiguities of the film even more intensely. The iconography of heroism is nourished by music, and looks more unstable and thus more interesting without it.
